title: The Feature Request Myth: What the Kano Model Says Customers Actually Notice

Noriaki Kano’s 1984 model explains which features earn delight, which only prevent anger, and which nobody will ever thank you for. Andrei-Nicusor Covalescu 5 min read · Oct 27, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by Frederick Adegoke Snr. on Pexels Clean sheets never got a hotel a five-star review. Dirty ones have sunk plenty. That small asymmetry is the whole idea behind one of the most useful and least discussed frameworks in product marketing: the Kano model. Most startups run on a quiet myth. The myth says customer happiness is a straight line: add a feature, get a bit more happiness. Fix a bug, get a bit more. Ship more, win more. In 1984, a Japanese quality researcher called Noriaki Kano and his colleagues published a paper, “Attractive Quality and Must-Be Quality”, that broke that line into pieces. Their point was simple and slightly uncomfortable. Some features make people happier the more you invest. Some only stop people from being angry. Some delight people precisely because nobody asked for them. And some don’t matter at all. If you treat all four the same, you’ll spend your roadmap in the wrong places. Myth 1: Every feature request is a vote for happiness The Kano model sorts features into five groups. Three of them do most of the work. Must-be features. These are the basics. Customers rarely mention them, and you get no credit for having them. You only hear about them when they’re missing. Clean sheets. A checkout that doesn’t crash. An invoice that adds up. Performance features. Also called one-dimensional. Here the line really is straight: more is better, less is worse. Faster delivery, more storage, lower price. This is where competitors compare you, feature by feature. Attractive features. The delighters. Customers don’t expect them, so their absence costs you nothing, but their presence creates a disproportionate “oh, nice” moment. The handwritten note in the box. The tool that fills in the form for you. The other two groups are indifferent features, which nobody cares about either way, and reverse features, which some customers actively dislike. Think of the “smart” autoplay that half your users rush to turn off. Here’s the trap. Customers mostly request performance features, because those are the ones they can name. They rarely request must-bes (they assume them) and almost never request delighters (they can’t imagine them). So a roadmap built only from feature requests tends to be a list of “a bit more of the same”. Myth 2: You can find out by asking “would you like this?” Ask anyone whether they’d like a feature and most will say yes. It costs them nothing. Kano’s questionnaire is cleverer. For each feature, you ask two questions: Functional: “If the product had this feature, how would you feel?” Dysfunctional: “If the product did not have this feature, how would you feel?” Each one gets the same five answers: I like it, I expect it, I’m neutral, I can live with it, I dislike it. The pair of answers tells you the category. A few common combinations: “I like it” if present, “I dislike it” if absent: performance . “I expect it” or “neutral” if present, “I dislike it” if absent: must-be . “I like it” if present, “neutral” or “I can live with it” if absent: attractive . “Neutral” both ways: indifferent . You run this across a sample of real customers, count the most common category for each feature, and suddenly your backlog has a shape. It’s not a perfect science, and small samples can mislead you, but it beats ranking features by who shouted loudest in the last sales call. Myth 3: A delighter stays a delighter This is the hidden gem of the model, and the part founders forget. Delight decays. What surprised people a few years ago becomes the thing they expect today. Free hotel Wi-Fi once felt like a gift. Now a hotel that charges for it gets complained about. Tracking a parcel in real time used to feel like magic. Now a shop without it feels sketchy. So the categories aren’t fixed. Attractive features drift into performance, and performance features drift into must-be. Your competitors copy your delighter, your customers get used to it, and it turns into a basic requirement you have to keep paying for. That’s why “we’re the only ones who do X” is a temporary position, not a strategy. The Kano model tells you to keep a small, steady budget for new delighters, because today’s surprise is next year’s baseline. A worked example from visas I lead marketing at Issa Compass , a legal-tech startup in Bangkok that helps people apply for Thai visas. Visa services are a useful lens for Kano because the must-bes are unusually heavy. Nobody gets excited that their visa paperwork is correct. They expect it. But a wrong document can wreck a move, so correctness sits firmly in must-be territory: invisible when it works, unforgivable when it doesn’t. No amount of nice design makes up for it. Performance features are the ones people compare: how quickly things move, how clearly the steps are explained, how easy it is to reach a human. And then there’s the room for delight. Issa Compass offers a free eligibility check, where people can see whether they meet the requirements for a specific visa before they commit.
